lesson_title: How a River Cuts Off Its Own Loop
hook_text: Rivers can cut off their own loops and leave lakes behind, overnight, in a single flood.
clip_script: Watch a river on flat land. It swings left, then right, in big loops called meanders. On the outside of each bend, fast water eats into the bank, making a steep cliff. On the inside, slow water drops sand, building a beach. So the loops keep growing, until one curls almost all the way round, like a snake biting its tail. A narrow neck of land is all that's left. Then a flood arrives. The water bursts straight across the neck. A short cut. The river takes it. Mud seals off the old loop, and what's left is a curved lake beside the river: an oxbow lake. Hippos, fish and birds move in. In KwaZulu-Natal, the Pongola River's flood plain is full of pans and lakes like this.
visual_style: An aerial view of a looping river; animated arrows showing fast water on outer bends and sand building on inner bends; a loop narrowing to a thin neck; floodwater bursting through; a horseshoe-shaped lake with birds and hippos.
pacing: Slow build as the loop grows, quick burst at the flood, calm finish at the lake.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson to learn how meanders and oxbow lakes form.
